prompt: Explain the difference between operational effectiveness and strategy (Porter 1996). Why is operational effectiveness not sufficient for a sustainable competitive advantage?
modelAnswer: Operational effectiveness means performing similar activities better than rivals – faster, cheaper, with fewer defects – which moves a firm towards the productivity frontier. Strategy means performing different activities or similar activities in a different way to deliver a unique mix of value. OE is not sufficient because best practices are quickly imitated: as everyone benchmarks, firms converge, the frontier shifts outward for all and nobody gains a relative advantage (competitive convergence). A sustainable advantage requires a unique position, trade-offs (what not to do) and fit among activities, which makes the whole system hard to imitate.
keyPoints: OE = same activities done better (productivity frontier)
Strategy = different activities / different ways, unique position
Trade-offs and fit make a position sustainable

prompt: Present Mintzberg's five Ps of strategy and explain the difference between deliberate and emergent strategies.
modelAnswer: Plan: a consciously intended course of action. Ploy: a manoeuvre to outwit a competitor. Pattern: consistency in behaviour over time, intended or not. Position: the place of the organization in its environment (its niche). Perspective: a shared, ingrained way of seeing the world (culture). Comparing plan and pattern gives the distinction: intended strategies that are realized are deliberate; intended strategies that are not realized are unrealized; realized strategies that formed without (or despite) intentions are emergent. In practice realized strategy mixes both, e.g. Honda's US success emerged and was later made deliberate.
keyPoints: Plan, ploy, pattern, position, perspective with a short meaning each
Emergent = realized pattern without prior intention
Example (e.g. Honda) or note that both are mixed

prompt: Why does the emergence of large organizations matter for strategy? Contrast the views of Chandler and Perrow.
modelAnswer: Chandler sees firms as engines of efficiency: railroads and the telegraph created volumes and speeds that markets could not coordinate, so firms that invested in large-scale plants, national distribution and professional management achieved high throughput and lower unit costs; structure follows strategy. Perrow argues that large organizations absorbed society: they also won because they kept the gains and externalized costs (accidents, unemployment, pollution) onto workers, communities and the state, and took over functions of family and community; networks of small firms would have been an alternative. Both agree organizations structure economic and social life – so the boundaries of the firm (what to internalize or outsource) are strategic choices with economic and social consequences, visible today in platforms and global value chains.
keyPoints: Chandler: administrative coordination, throughput, structure follows strategy
Perrow: society of organizations, externalized costs, alternative of small-firm networks
Boundaries of the firm are strategic choices with social consequences
